sections.title: The toll buyer: how a utility gets 3.6 GW of batteries without owning them
ps: The corpus now has four ways a regulated utility ends up with a battery on its system. Duke self-builds and signs the supply agreement. WEC buys a developer's finished project into {{rate base}} ({{build-transfer}}). DTE takes a customer's money and owns the plant. Arizona Public Service does none of these for most of its storage: it runs an {{all-source RFP}}, picks the winning bids, and signs a {{tolling agreement}} — a contract under which the developer builds, finances and owns the battery and APS pays a fixed fee for the right to charge and discharge it as it pleases for twenty years. The toller takes the market risk; the owner takes the availability risk. Of about 3,610 MW of storage APS signed from its 2023 solicitation, roughly 150 MW (the Agave project) is APS-owned. The rest sits on the balance sheets of Recurrent Energy, Strata Clean Energy, GridStor and developers not yet named.

This matters to a seller because it moves the buying decision one step away from the utility. The battery cells, the {{PCS}}, the enclosure and the {{EPC}} are chosen by the developer at bid stage, to hit a price the RFP will accept. APS never signs a battery purchase order; it signs a toll whose terms are the specification. The 2023 RFP asked for 365 equivalent cycles a year at a 50 percent average {{state of charge}} — a battery that is exercised once a day, every day, and rests half-full. That pair of numbers is what a bidder's warranty and augmentation plan have to cover, and it is the closest thing to a datasheet APS publishes.

The toll also explains what makes an APS project financeable. GridStor bought the 100 MW / 400 MWh White Tank project from Strata with the toll attached and, a year later, closed $220 million of construction financing from three banks. The lenders were pricing a twenty-year payment stream from a Baa1-rated utility, not a merchant battery's revenue forecast. Strata's business, as its own dossier records, is to win the toll, carry the project through interconnection and permitting, then sell it with the contract on — Scatter Wash to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, White Tank to GridStor. The toll is the asset; the battery is what it is attached to.

sections.title: The load-factor tariff: why a flat load gets its own rate schedule
ps: {{load factor}} is average demand divided by peak demand. A house that runs air-conditioning on summer afternoons and little at night might run at 30 percent; a data center that draws the same power every hour of the year runs above 90. The cost of serving a customer is dominated by the plant and wires sized to its peak, so two customers using the same energy cost very different amounts if one is peaky and one is flat. That is the logic behind APS's {{XHLF}} schedule, in force since March 2024: any customer above 5,000 kW whose load factor has held at 92 percent or better for nine of the last twelve months can take service at a lower energy rate ($0.04210 per kWh) with a demand charge of $18.750 per kW, because its kilowatts pay for themselves every hour.

What the schedule bundles with the price is the part a seller should read twice. The customer must sign an {{ESA}} that fixes contract length, minimum and maximum monthly loads and any special charges, and it pays a minimum bill for the term — the {{minimum demand charge}} idea in contract form. Above 15,000 kW it also pays contributions in aid of construction, a maintenance contract and a share of the cost of any facility the utility has to replace. What the schedule does not contain is an {{exit fee}}: the sheet has no early-termination payment, and no collateral formula. Those are the two terms every other utility in this corpus wrote into its 2025–2026 large-load tariff, and they are what APS's rate case and its 'subscription model' are adding now.

The subscription model is the contract form APS began describing in May 2026: individually negotiated XHLF agreements at cost-of-service prices, with a negotiated term, {{credit support}}, exit fees, and — the new element — the customer's option to contribute to financing or to accelerate key equipment such as substations and transformers, or to bring its own {{front-of-meter}} supply. It is WEC's {{bespoke resource}} arriving by contract instead of by tariff. Until the Corporation Commission's decision, expected by the end of 2026, the 4.5 GW APS calls committed is committed under ESAs written on the old sheet.

sections.title: Formula rates: the term the consumer parties fight hardest
ps: **The mechanism.** A traditional {{rate case}} sets prices from a historical {{test year}} and leaves them until the next case, so a utility whose {{rate base}} grows 7–9 percent a year earns below its {{allowed return}} in between — {{regulatory lag}}. A {{formula rate}} resets rates annually by formula from projected costs by customer class, closing the lag. APS's 2025 case asks for Arizona's first, the Formula Rate Adjustment Mechanism, alongside a 10.70 percent return (current 9.55) and a 14.69 percent day-one increase.

**Why it is contested.** The Residential Utility Consumer Office called it 'one, two, three or four increases on an annual basis' and asked instead for a separate data-center class; Commission Staff proposed a 9.55–9.80 percent return; the Attorney General argued for about 3 percent at a 6 percent return. Every consumer party accepts the large-load class; none accepts the annual reset. In a state with a five-member elected Commission, the formula rate is the politically exposed term, and its loss would cost more earnings than a lower return would.

**What a seller reads.** A utility that wins a formula rate can carry a bigger capital plan at the same credit metrics, which is where the Cholla conversion, the Redhawk expansion and the 'up to 2 GW' of new gas sit. A utility that loses it keeps buying capacity by toll — the cheapest route for its balance sheet — which is APS's model already.

sections.title: Committed and uncommitted: reading a queue against a peak
ps: APS publishes two numbers for its large-load book and a third that frames them. About 4.5 GW is 'committed' — under signed agreements and 'ramping up', in the CFO's words. About 20 GW is 'uncommitted' — requests in negotiation under the subscription model. And the 2025 system {{peak demand}} was 8.6 GW. The committed queue alone equals more than half of the system's peak; the uncommitted queue is two and a half times it. No other utility in this corpus shows a ratio like that: Dominion's contracted book is large but sits on a 20-plus GW system, and PPL Electric's 11 GW of signed agreements sits on a wires network in a market where it does not build the generation.

A queue is a claim on the peak, not on the energy. A data center at 92 percent load factor adds almost the same megawatts at the peak hour as at midnight, so 4.5 GW of committed load raises the capacity APS must have on the hottest afternoon by about 4.5 GW — before the 20 GW behind it. That is why the responses are all capacity: 380 MW at Cholla, the Redhawk expansion, a 2,000 MW gas plant proposed near Gila Bend, 3.6 GW of contracted batteries, and an anchor position on a 1.5 Bcf/d gas pipeline four years before the plants that will burn the gas. It is also why the 2035 forecast peak on APS's own page is 12.0 GW against 8.7 in 2025.

The ramp is the part a seller can watch. Commercial and industrial sales grew 12.7 percent in the second quarter of 2026 and 13.6 percent year to date — 'at or above the top end' of the 4–6 percent long-term rate APS guides for that class. TSMC's fabs are the one named source ('over 1 gigawatt'); 'half a dozen' data-center campuses are the rest, unnamed. When the committed number moves, a contract has been signed; when the C&I sales number moves, a contract has started to draw.

sections.title: Coal-to-gas on a brownfield: what Cholla buys and what it does not
sections.intro: APS retired its last Cholla coal unit in March 2025 and in July 2026 said it would convert two of the retired units to about 380 MW of gas by 2029, at up to $440 million. The cards compare that route with a new combined-cycle plant on an empty site.

sections.title: The desert summer: degree days, normalization and purchased power
ps: **The measurement.** A {{cooling degree day}} counts each degree the day's average temperature sits above 65°F. APS's second quarter of 2026 had 619 of them against 578 a year earlier — 7 percent more cooling demand from weather alone. Total retail sales rose 9.6 percent; {{weather-normalized}} sales rose 5.6 percent. The gap between the two numbers is the weather; the second number is the growth a seller should plan on.

**The supply.** In that quarter APS generated 5,962 GWh and bought 4,925 GWh — purchases up from 3,720 GWh a year earlier and now nearly half of supply. A utility that owns 6,257 MW against an 8.6 GW peak covers the gap with contracted plants (the tolls and PPAs) and with market purchases, and a hot quarter pushes more of the load onto the purchased side. Palo Verde ran at 86 percent for the quarter (a refuelling outage) and 92 percent for the half; the coal units ran at 64 percent.

**Why the miss.** Revenue rose $97 million and operating expenses rose $99 million: the cost of serving the extra load under rates set from a June 2022 test year exceeded what those rates recovered. That is regulatory lag in one quarter, and it is the case for the formula rate the company is asking for.

sections.title: Nuclear life extension: relicensing a plant you own a third of
ps: Palo Verde is three units of about 1,400 MW each west of Phoenix, owned by seven utilities; APS operates it and holds 29.1 percent — a 1,146 MW entitlement, the largest single block of firm capacity on its system. The units' current licenses run to the mid-2040s. In March 2026 APS said it would file a {{subsequent license renewal}} application in late 2027 to take each unit to 80 years: 2065, 2066 and 2067. Duke did the same for Oconee and Robinson; WEC achieved a similar result by contract, extending its Point Beach purchase to 2050. In every case the effect on the plan is identical — a gigawatt of baseload that would otherwise need replacing in the 2040s stays, and the capital plan does not have to grow to replace it.

The renewal has a cost that shows up in the capital plan now rather than later: about $200 million for a capacity buyout at Palo Verde and roughly $500 million over ten years, on the second-quarter 2026 slides. The application itself needs an aging-management review of the reactor vessels, containment and cables. The plant's water is 100 percent recycled wastewater from the Phoenix metro, and APS says operational water use has halved in ten years — the constraint a desert nuclear plant is judged on.

For a seller the reading is the same as at Duke and WEC. A utility that has decided to keep its nuclear for another twenty years has decided its next gigawatt of firm capacity will not be new nuclear and will not be a like-for-like replacement; what it still needs is capacity for the peak — the Cholla and Redhawk gas, the tolled batteries, the 2 GW program — and energy from the solar PPAs. The nuclear decision fixes the shape of everything else that gets bought.

sections.title: Gigawatts on the clock — the queue, the peak and the plan
sections.intro: APS's own figures at their most recent disclosure. The shape to notice: the committed queue is more than half the system peak, and contracted storage is twenty-four times the owned storage.
sections.note: The 2035 forecast peak on APS's data-center page is 12.0 GW against 8.7 GW in 2025; the total potential large load on the Q2 2026 slides is about 33 GW.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The queue does not convert.** The committed figure has read 'about 4.5 GW' from August 2025 to August 2026. If the Commission narrows the XHLF terms or rejects the formula rate in December 2026, the subscription contracts APS is negotiating lose their pricing basis and the 20 GW stays uncommitted.

**The customer mix is a single fab.** TSMC is the only named customer and a 'material portion' of the committed queue; the data-center campuses are unnamed. A semiconductor downturn would move APS's load forecast more than any one data center could.

**Tolls are only as good as the toller.** The 2023 RFP's projects are financed against APS's Baa1 rating and its right to recover the toll payments in rates; a rate outcome that disallows purchased-power cost, or a downgrade, would change what the next RFP's bidders can finance.

**Fuel arrives in 2029, the plants in 2030.** The 2 GW gas program depends on the Desert Southwest pipeline expansion; a slip in either moves the other, and the Cholla conversion (380 MW) is the only owned addition between Redhawk in 2028 and 2030.

cards.q: What is a tolling agreement, and who carries which risk?
cards.a: A contract under which a developer builds, owns and operates a battery and the utility pays a fixed fee for the right to charge and discharge it for the term — the utility (toller) takes the market risk, the owner takes the availability risk.

cards.q: Who chooses the battery OEM and the EPC on a tolled project?
cards.a: The developer, at bid stage, to hit the price the RFP will accept — the utility signs a toll, never a battery purchase order.

cards.q: What two numbers in the 2023 all-source RFP act as APS's battery specification?
cards.a: 365 equivalent cycles a year and a 50 percent average state of charge — one full cycle a day, resting half-full; the warranty and augmentation plan must cover them.

cards.q: What is load factor, and why does a 92 percent threshold earn a lower rate?
cards.a: Average demand divided by peak demand. A flat load uses the plant and wires sized to its peak every hour, so each kilowatt pays for itself; the energy rate can be lower because the capacity is fully used.

cards.q: Which two terms does the XHLF sheet lack that every 2025–2026 large-load tariff in the corpus carries?
cards.a: An exit fee (early-termination payment) and a collateral formula — the rate case and the subscription model are adding both.

cards.q: What does a formula rate change compared with a traditional rate case?
cards.a: Rates reset annually by formula from projected costs by class instead of waiting for the next contested case, closing regulatory lag; it is the term consumer parties oppose most.

cards.q: Why does a 4.5 GW committed queue matter more than 4.5 GW of energy sales?
cards.a: A flat load adds almost the same megawatts at the peak hour as at midnight, so it raises the capacity the utility must hold at the peak by nearly its full size — before the uncommitted queue behind it.

cards.q: What does converting a retired coal unit to gas buy that a greenfield plant does not?
cards.a: An existing interconnection, switchyard, water, site and permits — no interconnection queue — at a fraction of the capital; the cost is a capped output and an older cycle's efficiency.

cards.q: What is a cooling degree day, and why report weather-normalized sales beside actual sales?
cards.a: Each degree the day's average sits above 65°F counts one; a season's total measures weather-driven cooling load. Weather-normalized sales strip that out to show the growth new customers and new load actually produced.

cards.q: What does a subsequent license renewal do to a utility's capital plan?
cards.a: It keeps a block of firm baseload for twenty more years, so the plan does not have to replace it — the next firm capacity bought is for the peak (gas, tolled batteries), not like-for-like baseload.

The Palo Verde capacity buyout

The White Tank battery — it is APS-owned
